{{Short description|Statement about equivalence relations}}

In [[descriptive set theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], '''Silver's dichotomy''' (also known as '''Silver's theorem''')<ref name="Simpson87">S. G. Simpson, "Subsystems of Z<sub>2</sub> and Reverse Mathematics", p.442. Appearing in G. Takeuti, ''Proof Theory'' (1987), ISBN 0 444 87943 9.</ref> is a statement about [[Equivalence class|equivalence relations]], named after [[Jack Silver]].<ref name="YanfangThesis">L. Yanfang, [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/48655866.pdf On Silver's Dichotomy], Ph.D thesis. Accessed 30 August 2022.</ref><ref name="FriedmanConsistency">Sy D. Friedman, [https://www.infona.pl/resource/bwmeta1.element.bwnjournal-article-doi-10_4064-fm227-2-4 Consistency of the Silver dichotomy in generalized Baire space], Fundamenta Mathematicae (2014). Accessed 30 August 2022.</ref>

==Statement and history==
A relation is said to be [[Coanalytic set|coanalytic]] if its complement is an [[Analytic set|analytic]] set. Silver's dichotomy is a statement about the equivalence classes of a coanalytic equivalence relation, stating any coanalytic equivalence relation either has [[Countable|countably]] many equivalence classes, or else there is a [[perfect set]] of reals that are each incomparable to each other.<ref name="NewDirections">A. Kechris, [https://authors.library.caltech.edu/38629/1/421088.pdf New Directions in Descriptive Set Theory] (1999, p.165). Accessed 1 September 2022.</ref> In the latter case, there must be continuum many equivalence classes of the relation.<ref name="YanfangThesis" />

The first published proof of Silver's dichotomy was by Jack Silver, appearing in 1980 in order to answer a question posed by [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]].<ref name="Silver80">J. Silver, [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82744613.pdf Counting the number of equivalence classes of Borel and coanalytic equivalence relations] (Annals of Mathematical Logic, 1980, received 1977). Accessed 31 August 2022.</ref> One application of Silver's dichotomy appearing in recursive set theory is since equality restricted to a set <math>X</math> is coanalytic, there is no Borel equivalence relation <math>R</math> such that <math>(=\upharpoonright\aleph_0)\leq_B R\leq_B (=\upharpoonright 2^{\aleph_0})</math>, where <math>\leq_B</math> denotes [[Borel-reducibility | Borel equivalence relation]]. Some later results motivated by Silver's dichotomy founded a new field known as invariant descriptive set theory, which studies definable equivalence relations. Silver's dichotomy also admits several weaker recursive versions, which have been compared in strength with subsystems of second-order arithmetic from [[reverse mathematics]],<ref name="YanfangThesis" /> while Silver's dichotomy itself is provably equivalent to <math>\Pi_1^1\mathsf{-CA}_0</math> over <math>\mathsf{RCA}_0</math>.<ref name="Simpson87" />
